items.body: Review by The Progolyte — I had heard rumors in the community about this record being an underrated gem of the Rock Progressivo Italiano scene, so today I finally check it out. The record is called Flore Di Metallo by I Califfi, and overall I got some really nice vibes from this one. While it may not be top-tier in the world of Italian prog, it's got some really nice keyboard-based rock music with a nice twinge of excitement oozing out of it. The cover didn't seem to convey the musical identity that much, with the more moody atmosphere I got from it, but that part of this album was still pretty good as well. Moving on, I really enjoyed the musicianship and thought the personnel had a lot of talent being the classic four-man crew. It includes Sandro Cinotti on keyboards, Vincenzo Amadei on guitar, Franco Boldrini on bass, Maurizio Boldrini on drums, and then all but Sandro helps out with the vocals. The music is quite strong, having an ear-catching mix of hard rock and symphonic prog. You also get some acoustic bits on songs like Alleluia and Felicit�, Sorriso E Pianto, which seem to fit in as a counter to the much more erratic styles on other pieces. The songs do seem to be a little shorter than what I would like, but the material here is strong enough to make up for the lacking lengths. These guys sound very similar to Quella Vecchia Locanda at points, specifically the more rock-focused bits of their debut album, though they still have those classical elements floating around here and there. Tracks like Flore Finto, Flore Di Metallo, and Varius are some of the most exciting, bombastic, and interesting compositions on the album. They approach heavy jazz fusion and avant prog at points while also playing into more somber and moody tones. Other highlights on the album include the opener Nel Mio Passato and Campane, which have some really nice depth along with beginning and ending the record nicely. In conclusion, I enjoyed this one quite a bit, and I'll definitely be coming back to it more often. It's incredibly engaging with the listener and always delving deep into the musical environment of the fusions of heavy psych and wild symphonic prog, and I hope more people listen to this one soon enough. As for my final rating, I think I'll go with a mid or strong 4/5.
items._cn_summary: 意大利前卫摇滚专辑，发行于1973年，属于Rock Progressivo Italiano流派。作品以键盘为核心，融合硬摇滚、交响元素与爵士融合风格，展现出跨领域的音乐特征。乐评指出其受Quella Vecchia Locanda影响，但融入了古典与爵士元素，在部分曲目中呈现重爵士融合与前卫倾向。专辑包含原声段落与情绪化表达，音乐编排在情绪起伏间保持张力。作为70年代意大利地下音乐场景的作品，其在实验性与传统交响语汇间寻找平衡，具有一定的创新价值。整体而言，这是一张融合多元素的扎实意大利前卫摇滚作品，适合对跨界融合和欧洲复古实验音乐感兴趣的听众。

items.body: Here, he stands swallowed by the sky Life, so small – dust in nature’s eye He seeds the ground, fallow by death’s hand Our hidden past, the fiction of all man L’Avenir has ushered in their latest album, Secrets, with the video for Animism, a coldwave séance of mineral calm and occult motion, where the air seems to have been left under overnight under a full moon, and returned with new intelligence. The Baltimore project, led by Jason Sloan, treats electronic music as architecture as much as emotion: a corridor of blue light, a stairwell descending beneath memory, a voice arriving from somewhere just beyond the visible wall. On this first single from the project’s eighth album, Sloan works with a familiar vocabulary: patient drum-machine pressure, icy synthesizers, distant singing – but the result feels newly charged, as if each element has been placed glowing under glass. Animism takes its title with admirable seriousness. The song imagines a world in which matter has memory and the inanimate keeps counsel. The earth, the tree, the old room, the object handled too often by human longing: all seem to possess a private pulse. Sloan’s voice sits inside the track rather than above it, less a guide than a presence caught in the same current as the listener. The effect is intimate and estranged, the sound of someone speaking from within a thought that has become physical. The track brings to mind the elegant austerity of Eleven Pond, the dusky romanticism of Clan of Xymox, the severe European mechanics of Parade Ground, and the cerebral chill of Trisomie 21. These references move through the song like figures glimpsed in frosted glass, recognizable but never allowed to dominate the room. The arrangement advances with a measured hand, giving each synth line and percussive motion enough space to breathe before the next cold gleam arrives. The accompanying video, directed by Soleil Noir Studios, deepens the spell. Shot by Jason Sloan, with Sloan also handling video synthesizer programming and both analogue and digital hardware, the clip turns the forests of the mind into a prismatic terrain. Bright colours bloom against mirrored images; faces and forms double, dissolve, and reassemble in a kind of psychic woodland. The imagery suggests a psychedelic passage through inner nature, where branches become nerves, light becomes thought, and perception starts to behave like a living organism. Animism presents L’Avenir as a project still devoted to solitude, mystery, and nocturnal design, but newly attentive to the strange life hidden inside surfaces. Sloan makes darkwave feel porous here, open to trees, stones, ghosts, and the quiet intelligence of everything we mistakenly believe is still. Watch the video for “Animism” below: Secrets is out now via EINS:ZWEI:ACHT on vinyl, CD, digital, and streaming formats. Listen to Animism below and order Secrets here. items._cn_summary: 巴尔的摩冷潮计划L'Avenir的第八张专辑《Secrets》首支单曲《Animism》，将暗潮与电子声响相融合，创造出冷冽而富有灵性的音乐空间。专辑以万物有灵论为概念，将合成器、鼓机与人声编织成隐秘的建筑般结构。评论中将其与Eleven Pond、Clan of Xymox等暗潮经典进行比较，同时强调其在传统暗潮语汇上的新突破。视频由Soleil Noir Studios执导，呈现超现实的心理景观。作为独立发行作品，其在暗潮与电子实验的交汇处找到了独特的表达方式，符合用户对暗潮及电子音乐口味的偏好，整体具有较高的艺术完成度与创新意识。

items.body: You wanna know your problem is? Well, don’t ask me. I’m not your Shrink. Spike Hellis returns with No Bite, and the joke is already grinning at you before the first beat has exploded. The Los Angeles duo’s second preview of Successor, due August 7 via Over-Pop, arrives like a chrome-plated insult with a cigarette burn on its tongue: lean, clipped, mean, and menacing. They ain’t your therapists, that’s for sure. This is body music, with its teeth filed to points, though the title would have you believe otherwise. No Bite rides a soft jackhammer groove, sparse, minimalist industrial EBM, and dry, mechanical funk. Cortland Gibson and Lainey Chang refrain from overpacking the track by letting the empty space do some of the dirty work. The beat hits, withdraws, hits again, and every pause feels like somebody waiting for you to flinch. There is a special cruelty in restraint. Plenty of bands in this lane mistake volume for violence, pile on distortion until everything becomes an expensive blur, and then wonder why nobody looks afraid. No Bite‘s power comes from precision: the bassline’s blunt insistence, the synths’ clipped little wounds, the vocal delivery moving around the track like a bored predator tapping the glass. You can hear the old EBM gods rattling around in the pipes, but this is no Wax Trax! museum march. It has the nasty modern confidence of a duo that has spent time in real rooms, under real lights, with real bodies pressed against the pit fence. Gibson and Chang have shared stages with Front 242 and Nitzer Ebb, and No Bite channels that lineage, evoking a room where fog juice hangs in your hair, and the dancefloor has absorbed enough questionable decisions to qualify as a legal witness. The track is compact, confrontational, and just a little unstable, thudding away in the dark on spite alone. Listen to No Bite below and order the single here. No Bite by Spike Hellis Spike Hellis will release their second studio album, Successor, on August 7 via Over-Pop, with No Bite serving as its second preview after By God. The roadwork begins just ahead of the album’s release, kicking off July 31 in Santa Ana before stretching across the Southwest, Texas, the South, the East Coast, Canada, the Midwest, and the Pacific Northwest, eventually circling back to California for an October 24 hometown-area close in Los Angeles. They’ll be joined along the way by MVTANT, Auragraph, Belly Hatcher, Nuxx, and Normal Bias. items.body: In the distance I am cold In the distance We’re growing old Casket Cassette’s Show Me a Sign is a song that illuminates the soul like a busted strip of Los Angeles nightlife, all neon nerves and cheap salvation. Constant Laval Williams has made a fine little art out of sounding stranded in public, which is harder than it sounds. Plenty of singers can do lonely. Fewer can do lonely while the beat is still carrying everybody’s boots across the dancefloor. This is the third new song from REDUCER, out June 12. Show Me a Sign is all reduction: emotion boiled until it stains the pan, desire shaved down to the bare request, survival turned into something blunt enough to fit in one hand. There is no grand cathedral of misery here, no velvet cape dragged theatrically through dry ice. The song wants a signal, a room, a body, a way back from whatever distance has turned the song’s protagonist cold and old before his time. Show Me a Sign channels the Medusa, Twist of Shadows, and Creatures era Clan of Xymox in its dusky romantic architecture, Cold Cave in its sleek black propulsion, and the frozen passion of The Danse Society and Pink Turns Blue, but Casket Cassette is smart enough to understand that influences should behave like a ghost at the bar, present but never picking up the tab. And the track moves with the clean, severe confidence of a dark priest descending inward into an icy sanctum, torchlit and severe, conjuring unspeakable visions as Williams’ voice cuts through the darkness. Lyrically, the song circles distance, exhaustion, and the stubborn will to continue after comfort has abandoned the room. The plea for a sign feels less like romantic longing than a last candle held against the cold, a small act of devotion made under pressure. Casket Cassette turns that ache into body music for the damaged and devout, for people who have been through Hell and back again and lived to tell the tale. Mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios and mastered by Stefan Brown at Abbey Road Studios, Show Me a Sign has a polished chill; every element has been placed with surgical precision: the beat advances, the synths flare and recede, and the vocal keeps its eyes open. The song’s desperation lands because it is sharpened rather than softened, with the production giving the plea force, shape, and urgency. Listen to Show Me a Sign below and order the single here. Show Me a Sign by Casket Cassette Casket Cassette will take The Reducer Tour across North America in summer 2026, with support from Stare Away and special guests. The run opens in Southern California before cutting through the Southwest and Texas, heading up the East Coast, crossing into Toronto, then moving through the Midwest, Mountain West, Pacific Northwest, and back down the West Coast, with a final date in California in November. items._cn_summary: Casket Cassette的单曲《Show Me a Sign》属于暗潮与后朋克交汇的声音景观，完全契合用户的核心音乐偏好。乐评详尽分析了歌曲如何将Clan of Xymox、Cold Cave、The Danse Society等先驱的影响融入自身表达，同时保持克制与精准的美学姿态。作品以精简的编曲策略呈现情感张力，歌词围绕疏离、疲惫与生存意志展开主题，制作层面由Abbey Road Studios的Stefan Brown进行母带处理保证了声音质量。对于关注暗潮与后朋克领域的听众而言，这是一部值得关注的独立发行作品。

items.excerpt: Remy and Pascal Le Boeuf, twin brothers from Santa Cruz who have teamed up to release six albums that embrace their jazz upbringing and venture bravely into contemporary classical and indie-rock realms, are currently at the top of their game as composers...
items.body: Remy and Pascal Le Boeuf, twin brothers from Santa Cruz who have teamed up to release six albums that embrace their jazz upbringing and venture bravely into contemporary classical and indie-rock realms, are currently at the top of their game as composers, having recently won individual Grammy Awards for Best Instrumental Composition. The upcoming Le Boeuf Brothers album Off Center, a follow-up to their whisper-quiet 2023 recording HUSH, jacks up the excitement factor with a program of all-original material that goes even further in engaging the simpatico members of their quintet, which includes alto saxophonist Remy and pianist Pascal joined by longtime co-conspirators Dayna Stephens (tenor saxophone), Linda May Han Oh (bass) and Christian Euman (drums). It's an all-acoustic affair that finds the group leaning into spontaneity and elasticity in search of the unconventional, stretching the compositions (six by Pascal, five by Remy) far beyond what's written on the page in a delightful adventure of shared risk and mutual trust. The Le Boeufs — who became involved with high-profile West Coast educational jazz programs at a young age, attended Manhattan School of Music and went on to get advanced degrees — have carved out neat career paths of their own. They have each produced significant bodies of work, releasing their own recordings as bandleaders, attaining high-level job roles in prominent educational institutions, garnering awards galore and delivering masterful compositions in connection with commissions and grants. And let's not forget their well-honed chops, in-the-moment instincts and their seemingly second-nature ability to navigate and manipulate chord changes while improvising — qualities that come to prominence in this quintet environment and set in motion the more exciting and engaging aspects of Off Center. Since even before the 2009 release of their debut recording, House Without A Door, Remy and Pascale Le Boeuf have constituted one of the most compelling creative partnerships in jazz and contemporary music. They have developed into essential contributors to the modern jazz canon, and are well worth checking out on record and in live performance. Upcoming tour dates for Le Boeuf Brothers include shows on June 5 at Sam First in Los Angeles, June 6 at Kuumbwa Jazz Center in Santa Cruz, California, and June 7 at the Palo Alto Art Center Auditorium in Palo Alto, California.
items._cn_summary: Le Boeuf Brothers 双胞胎兄弟的最新专辑《Off Center》延续其融合爵士、当代古典与独立摇滚的创作风格。专辑由 Pascal 与 Remy 共同创作，两位自幼接受 West Coast 爵士教育并获得 Manhattan School of Music 高学历背景。五重奏编制包含 Dayna Stephens、Linda May Han Oh 与 Christian Euman，演奏强调自发性和弹性，将作曲框架延伸至传统记谱之外。全原创作曲共十一首，融合学院派爵士的即兴精髓与实验性探索。虽然为纯原声音乐而非电子元素，但专辑对声音边界的拓展和对常规的突破，符合实验性爵士的审美取向。DownBeat 刊载的评论显示该作已获专业认可，整体艺术性与用户偏好的实验爵士与当代古典方向高度契合。

items.excerpt: Wolfgang Muthspiel has been plying his creativity at the guitar for a dedicated, long time in nearly a dozen configurations as a leader — everything from solo works to big band extravaganzas to trio settings...
items.body: Wolfgang Muthspiel has been plying his creativity at the guitar for a dedicated, long time in nearly a dozen configurations as a leader — everything from solo works to big band extravaganzas to trio settings, especially trio settings. There's his work with the MGT trio (with Slava Grigoryan and Ralph Towner), another with Larry Grenadier and Brian Blade, then the work he did with Brad Mehldau and Ambrose Akinmusire and the Autria String Trio (with Benjamin Schmid and Florian Eggner. All of them satisfying. But just as satisfying is the new Wolfgang Muthspiel Chamber Trio recording, Atlas. In describing the group on his website, Muthspiel says the goal of the group "is to create an interactive, polyphonic musical network that embraces the intimacy and transparency of chamber music formations without sacrificing rhythmic power or a sense of playful improvisation." It's fascinating what this combination of Muthspiel on guitars, Mario Rom on trumpet and Colin Vallon on piano can do. This isn't what one might think of as a chamber group. They dispense with the pomp and politeness of classical music to focus on sound, improvisation and creativity. Take, for instance, the album's fourth cut, "Lionel," an obvious ode to Lionel Loueke, another trio collaborator (with Linda May Han Oh on the album Confluence.) The tune opens with Muthspiel rhythmically scraping the strings and using the guitar's body as a percussion instrument to introduce a heartbeat before Rom and Vallon come in with the melody. There's one foot in etude-land and another in modern jazz improvisation and just a touch of the flavor of mother Africa. Vocals, sweet and simple, come into the sound palette, and then at about the 6 minute mark the beauty is interrupted by a furious lash of electric guitar theatrics in a way that catches the listener off guard, but makes perfect sense. The playing on this album is beautiful. Muthspiel's acoustic guitar work on songs like "Gaucho Shubert," the opening track, just glisten. With overdubs, pure flights of technical precision and in-the-moment soloing, there's so much to like on this recording. And massive thanks to the team that recorded, mixed and mastered this work. The sound is as impeccable as the musicianship.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑出自奥地利吉他手沃尔夫冈·穆特施皮尔领导的室内爵士三重奏，与小号手马里奥·罗姆和钢琴家科林·瓦隆合作。音乐融合了古典室内的透明质感与爵士乐的即兴张力，突破了传统室内乐的端庄框架，强调声音质感、节奏力量与自由演奏的平衡。专辑中可听到非洲音乐元素的微妙影响，如打击乐式的吉他演奏和人声点缀，展现出跨界融合的实验性。录音与制作质量上乘，吉他与小号的声部层次清晰。该作品在ECM厂牌发行，虽属主流爵士唱片公司，但音乐本身具有较高的艺术价值和实验精神，契合用户对学院派爵士和现代作曲风格的偏好。

items.body:
Sooraj Sivadas aka MONé's debut album 'Lucid Dreams' is laced through and through with extremely hard-hitting kicks and soft pads, and everything in the distance between the aforementioned two's visceral and ethereal extremes is filled with sounds that fizzle and distort.

The first proper musical opening on the album, 'Cornucopia' (the preceding actual opener 'Whisper' serves more as an ambient skit explaining the album's concept and title with a voice recording), introduces this sonic world best as it starts with the reverberating expanse of deep techno before its spaces get filled with a deluge of atonal synth, metallic textures and the buzzing reactions between the two.

The Kerala-rooted producer-DJ combines metallic, machine-like precision in drums with glitchy, swaying percussive sounds on 'Sanctuary' and 'Starseed', or, more often, the syncopation of breakbeats on tracks like 'Kill Time' and 'Therefore I Am'. The combination brings both warmth and coldness while operating in the dark bass-heavy echelons of dance music around techno and beyond. 'Kill Time' even hints at dubstep with its half-time sway and low-pressure basslines before surprising with the breakneck rhythmic onslaught of drum 'n' bass. Both qualities carry over to the album's most hypnotic number 'Stand By', a highlight on the 11-track record, which nearly steps into trance territory with its immersive pulsating textures, were it not for the surprises of the breakbeats and industrial percussion.

Evidently, it is a record with multiple influences and MONé's maximalist streak does continue. However, none of the 11 tracks leaves the sonic world built across the album or puts its outlined concept (through the starting track and album title) into question. 'Lucid Dreams' is an undoubtedly cohesive journey just for someone with the apetite to revel in the intensity and energy that it has to offer.

Listen to the album below and head to MONé's artist profile for more.
items._cn_summary: 印度制作人MONé的首张专辑，将techno、drum 'n' bass、dubstep与industrial元素融合。专辑以深邃的techno底色为起点，叠加glitch质感的打击乐、断裂式breakbeats与金属化合成音色。作品在黑暗低音与冰冷机械节奏中注入温暖与暖度，同时保留了极端声响设计的实验性。Kerala根源赋予其独特的文化视角，使暗潮、工业与电子舞曲的跨界融合更具原创性。最大亮点在于节奏的不确定性——dubstep半速摇摆与drum 'n' bass高速冲击的并置，以及trance氛围与工业打击的意外碰撞。11首曲目构成连贯的整体，呈现出一个完整而密集的声音世界，适合追求高强度实验舞曲的听者。

items.body: Eight kilometres outside Essaouira, between the douar of Ghazoua and the surf break at Sidi Kaouki, there is a family house named after a Corsican village in Balagne. That is where HabibiSly filmed his debut single, after discovering Gnawa music and following it to Essaouira. Rabbath is the Paris-born son of the Syrian-French double bassist François Rabbath, trained at the Nadia et Lili Boulanger conservatoire and then taken on the road for twenty-five years across four continents at his father’s side. His own project runs on synths, piano, and talkbox, absorbing the Levantine modes of his upbringing through the club nights of Paris’s 18th arrondissement. “Dar Algajola” is the first single from his debut EP Habibi Rhapsody, due in September on Heavenly Sweetness, directed and produced as a video by Athys de Galzain on location in Essaouira, where he records with Saad Tiouly, a young Casablanca maâlem, guembri player and Gnawa singer who has spent years working inside the tradition before pushing it outward into folk, rock and Mediterranean territory, and Aziz Atmani, a Moroccan gnaoui who blends traditional North African sounds with electronic and ambient music. The guembri’s three-string bass drone and the iron clatter of the krakebs sit inside Rabbath’s synthesiser beds, the Gnawa call-and-response riding over programmed percussion, the talkbox bending between Arabic and club frequencies. Gnawa ceremony is built to keep going until the room changes state. This track is built the same way. items._cn_summary: HabibiSly的《Dar Algajola》将摩洛哥 Gnawa 传统音乐与电子合成器、talkbox效果以及俱乐部节拍相融合。Rabbath在巴黎积累了深厚的学院音乐训练背景，其项目以合成器垫底、guembri三弦低音长音和krakebs铁器敲击的节奏为核心，配合Gnawa式的呼叫应答唱法。talkbox在阿拉伯语与电子频率之间弯折，Saad Tiouly和Aziz Atmani两位摩洛哥音乐人的参与确保了Gnawa传统的真实性。这首单曲体现了世界音乐与电子音乐的跨领域融合，具有实验性色彩，同时保持了北非传统音乐的地域特色。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — The Basque culture that straddles the northeastern part of Spain and southwestern region of Francehas fascinated linguists and anthropologists alike owing to the fact that this culture appears to beone of the last remnants of Paleolithic Europe before the arrival of the Indo-Europeans. Given thisculture's rather isolate position in terms of its relationship amongst other European cultures, it'slittle wonder that it too has developed some of its own unique musical styles. While little known tothe outside world, the Basque region did indeed participate in the flavorful sounds that emergedduring the psychedelic and progressive years and thanks to DJ Makala who compiled a number of tracksfrom various artists, this excellent compilation is like a box of assorted chocolates awaiting yourdiscovery.KATEBEGIAK Prog-Rock, Psych-Folk & Jazz-Rock Music from the Basque Country was released in 2021 andhighly acclaimed for showcasing some of the region's history that was the crucial link thatconnected the folk revivalists of the 1960s and the Basque Radical Rock (Euskal Herriko rockerradikala) that fueled the regions punk scene. The term KATEBEGIAK actually means "Links of achain." The album features 13 select tracks that display the wide array of experimental sounds thatsprang up in the 1970s and continued into the 80s. After the 60s revival movement, bands began tocross-pollinate their homegrown folk music with the various forms of psychedelia, rock and jazzfusion that were springing up all around Europe and the world since the mid-1960s and this Whitman'ssample pack is the perfect place to dip in and get a taste of such sounds for further exploration.This release features all the expected artists such as the most popular Basque act Itoiz as well asHaizea, Enbor and Errobi but also features some of the rarest of the rare with bands such as thePamplona based Magdalena and the virtually unknown Urria. Strangely this collection features arather interesting choice of what to include and what not as it features the track "Pello Joxepe"which as an outlier from rest and features a Mississippi born black psychedelic soul singer coveringa traditional Basque song and yet the release doesn't include real Basque acts that existed at thetime including Sakre, Akelarre, Mirotz and Patxi Villamor. Track lengths vary considerably as wellranging from the 3 1/2 minute "Agurra II" from Enbor to the longest track "Andere" from Errobi whichsprawls out to 13 1/2 minutes. While these acts varied widely in approach, the thread that keeps it all connected is the softsensual folk and oft flute oriented music that in some ways resembles Celtic folk music but soundsas distinct as the language this unique population has kept alive despite all odds. Some of thetrack placements are a bit odd as the opening "Egunaren Hastapena" by Haizea takes a good fiveminutes to slowly work up to some sort of song structure. The following "Xori Bele" by Izkaitzwould've been a better choice as it provides a more direct introduction into the culturalsmorgasbord about to be experience however this is hardly a deal breaker as all the tracks areworthy of an attentive listen. While most of these artists are clearly more in the psychedelic folk camp with touches of prog rockin for the mix, bands like Lisker actually deliver the more rocking bravado whereas the tracks byAmala Zubrina & Pascual Gaigne along with the album's closer by Urria are extremely ethereal and themost experimental. Despite the urge to play these in a different order it's the music that countsand although i've heard of many of these bands i haven't actually heard them so this is the perfectway to get acquainted as well as finding some rarities that have completely escaped the attention ofeven the most sleuth oriented databases. The Basque scene was quite distinct from the Rock Andaluzand jazz fusion scenes of the rest of Spain and this compilation is the perfect way to explore thisoften neglected region of the nation. Pretty much every track works for me however i wish theexcluded acts were on this one too.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自巴斯克地区的精选合辑，收录1972至1985年间当地渐进摇滚、迷幻民谣与爵士摇滚的代表性作品。专辑汇集了Itoiz、Haizea、Enbor、Errobi等重要乐队，并包含一些极为稀有的资料。音乐核心特征是将巴斯克传统民谣与欧陆迷幻运动、爵士融合进行跨文化混响，曲目时长达13分余，呈现实验性编排。巴斯克语演唱与独特的民族乐器运用（如长笛）构成鲜明的地方色彩。作为独立发行的考古式合辑，其价值在于呈现欧洲边缘地区的前卫音乐探索史，对于关注实验融合与世界音乐交叉地带的听众具有较高的参考意义。

items.body: Review by TenYearsAfter — Ruud Dielen had a long history with cover bands , playing guitar in songs from Jimi Hendrix, Santana, Led Zeppelin, Queen, Toto and Genesis. After many years touring in the more commercial circuit, he decided that it was time to write his own music and in 2017 he produced his first album entitled Aquarius, as a one-man-band (guitar, bass and synthesizers), under the name Glorious Wolf. The music sounds as a tribute to the Seventies era progrock and Classic Rock, from Pink Floyd to Zappa and Hendrix, embellished with a wonderful array of vintage sounds (from Moog, Mellotron and Hammond to Gibson, Fender and Mesa Boogie). On his second album Zodiac (2019) and third Mysterious Traveller (2023) Ruud started to invite male and female singers, and to blend the progrock sound with a more song-oriented and varied musical attitude. On Prog Archives Ruud Dielen his Glorious Wolf project got a lot of praise for that musical formula, meandering tastefully and elaborately between instrumental Old School vintage keyboard drenched progrock and song-oriented tracks. And now, anno 2026, here's Ruud again (playing acoustic - and electric guitars, fretless bass, Precision bass, synthesizers, mellotron and FX drums) with Glorious Wolf, featuring a range of national and international guest musicians, on vocals, drums, bass, Hammond, Yamaha piano, Mellotron, theremin and saxophone. Most of the foreign musicians Ruud had met during an international musical collaboration.Elements of Hope Pt.1 ? Instrumental (4.34) : This new album starts with an exciting electronic music atmosphere featuring pulsating sequencers and spacey synthesizers, then howling and biting Gilmourian guitar runs, topped with Mellotron choirs, followed by a tight and catchy beat. The music is embellished with Ruud his powerful guitar runs, fat synthesizer flights and soaring Mellotron choirs, and backed by a fluent rhythm-section (Kike Paglia on drums and Tim Ros on bass). In the end majectic Mellotron choirs erupt, wow, what an impressive start!Elements of Hope Pt.2 - Carrying this Yoke (6.15) : The intro delivers psychedelic sounding Mellotron violins. The music turns into a folky climate with acoustic guitar and fragile English male vocals (by Frank van der Borg), in a slow rhythm. Gradually a more lush sound featuring Mellotron violins, and powerful vocals and guitar riffs. In the final part a break with raw guitar riffs and propulsive drum beats. Lots of contrast, variety and dynamics, and tastefully arranged.Elements of Hope Pt.3 - Into the Clouds (5.55) : First celestial female vocals (by Jyoti Verhoeff) and twanging acoustic guitar, in a dreamy and hypnotizing climate, wonderful. Now the sound becomes more lush, embellished with fretless bass, slow drumbeats and distinctive female vocals. Gradually the atmosphere is working to a symptuous climax with a synthesizer solo, powerful drums and Hammond, culminating into fiery guitar solo, how exciting.Elements of Hope Pt.4 ? Instrumental (1.42) : A short piece in an ominous climate, with raw and powerful guitar, and slow and powerful drumbeats, the interplay is awesome.Elements of Hope Pt.5 - Life's Chaotic Spell (5.51) : The final part of this 5-pieve epic title track contains omnipresent Hammond, blended with exciting rock guitar, powerful male English vocals and a propulsive rhythm-section. Now saxophone play (by Reg Parham) joins, strongly coloring the music, with hints from Frank Zappa and King Crimson. Finally a heavy guitar solo, backed by a dynamic rhythm-section and Hammond.If You Please ? instrumental (6.20) : This composition delivers a slow rhythm and a compelling climate, Ruud really shines with his guitarwork, from sensitive to fiery, and using the tremolo-arm and wah-wah pedal, prog meets bluesrock, wow. Halfway beeps and bleeps, then a more atmospheric sound featuring spectacular wah-wah driven guitar runs, backed by propulsive drumbeats.If I Only (5.46) : After an intro with Mellotron (by the late Thomas Zunk) and militairy drums the music turns into a slow rhythm with heavy guitar, strong male vocals and gradually a more bombastic atmosphere. Halfway a fiery guitar solo, with howling and biting leads and Hammond layers, the music builds and builds, very compelling and exciting.Whirlwinds & Maelstroms ? instrumental (6.44) : Another Mellotron soaken intro, then slow drumbeats and powerful guitar. Halfway a swirling Hammond solo (XK5 Hammond with Leslie by Harry Knapen), followed by a heavy guitar solo, the interplay is excellent.Everything Must Break to Grow - EoH Pt.2 Reprise (6.25) : The final track on this new album starts with dreamy piano and vocals, then a slow rhythm, in a melancholical atmosphere, topped with subtle slide guitar. Gradually the sound turns into more lush and powerful featuring rock guitar and a dynamic rhythm-section. Finally dreamy with spacey synthesizers, guitar and voices, another example of Ruud his interesting and varied musical ideas.In the 3 years after his previous effort Ruud has moved and built a high-tec studio in his new home. You can hear the result: a mature and elaborate new album on which the music is wonderfully meandering between Old School prog and a more varied and song-oriented musical approach, embellished with his awesome guitarwork, vintage keyboards and vocal leads, and backed by good musicians. After Edo Spanninga (as E.D.O.) with his solo album The Past Is A Foreign Country, his other project Trion with Terra Tiempo here is another excellent new Dutch prog effort, well done Ruud!
items._cn_summary: 这是一张融合七十年代复古音色与现代电子元素的前卫摇滚专辑，由荷兰音乐人Ruud Dielen主导。专辑以Crossover Prog为核心风格，巧妙融合了经典摇滚、电子音乐和艺术摇滚元素，在器乐演奏与歌曲导向之间自如切换。评论者强调其复古音色（如Moog、Mellotron、Hammond）与电子音乐氛围的结合，以及在传统与现代之间的平衡。专辑邀请了多位客座音乐人，涵盖人声、鼓、贝斯、键盘等多种乐器，呈现出丰富的层次感。对于偏好实验和前卫风格的用户而言，这种融合复古与实验元素的前卫摇滚具有较高的匹配度，创新性和独特性都较为突出。整体而言，这是一张兼具艺术性与可听性的作品，适合对跨界融合和实验性音乐感兴趣的听众。

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Empath' is undoubtedly one of the most eclectic and unbridled albums Devin Townsend has everrecorded. Conceived as some sort of magnum opus, this 2019 release encompasses a diverse range ofmusical influences from the Canadian musician's extensive back catalogue - everything from blastingavant-garde metal and progressive rock to symphonic music, ambient, and dance-pop (well, the lastone is a bit ironic, but you get the picture) is part of this ambitious and maximalist progexcursion. A huge, bold, and resonant work of art, 'Empath' is to my understanding a celebration ofthe musical universe of Devin Townsend, with all of its quirky, corny, overblown and elementalfacets. Joined by co-produced Mike Keneally, this record features a rather impressive set of guestmusicians and contributors, too, including the likes of Adam "Nolly" Getgood of Periphery who isresponsible for engineering and mixing the album, drummer Morgan �gren of Kaipa who has somesongwriting credits, and Steve Vai, among many others, who contributes a flamboyant guitar solo atthe very end of the album.Made up of ten album tracks, each song on 'Empath' explores a particular corner of the DevinTownsend sound. Opener 'Genesis', with its prelude 'Castaway', is a quirky piece of prog rock withcomplex, wacky arrangements, heavy guitars and a string of surprising sounds, and for many one ofthe most representative Devin pieces on this album. 'Spirits Will Collide' then follows up with abeautifully orchestrated triumphant sound, while the fourth track 'Evermore' marks a return to thedense and heavy sound that we're more familiar with. Stylistically, this song reminisces theuplifting prog metal Townsend had explored on his 2009 album 'Addicted'. We then have the excellent'Sprite', which is one of the more experimental entries on 'Empath', combining seamlessly electronicsynth sounds with winding symphonic music. 'Hear Me' is a manic piece of metal (think of SYL as areference), and unlike the classically-inspired song 'Why?', captures one of the most maximalist DTperformances on this record. The 11-minute-long 'Borderlands', which is the next major highlight, isa really playful piece of energetic prog metal, only followed by the six-part suite 'Singularity',sitting at twenty-three-plus minutes of playtime. Featuring a string of complex shifts and thetypical Wall of sound style of production, this is one of the most powerful and angular epicsrecorded by Townsend, and while parts of it are really impressive, I would hardly call it theperfect epic as it can occasionally feel a bit too hectic and immense.Nevertheless, 'Empath' is a fabulous solo album from Devin Townsend that aims to represent the all-encompassing nature of his music, uniting together on the same record the full range of musicalinfluences that make up his world. Surely one of the impressive and memorable releases of 2019.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张高度实验性的前卫金属专辑，融合了重金、古典交响、电子合成和实验音乐等多种元素，充分体现了Devin Townsend的音乐世界。专辑包含从激烈的前卫金属到优雅的交响乐段，再到电子氛围和舞曲元素的跨界尝试，曲目安排上既有直接强劲的作品，也有长达二十多分钟的结构复杂套曲。由Mike Keneally共同制作，并邀请了Steve Vai等知名音乐人参与，整体制作水准和艺术视野都相当突出。对于偏好实验和前卫风格的用户而言，这张专辑在风格匹配度和创新性上都达到了较高水准。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The third and final part of Gong's Radio Gnome Invisible trilogy, where Zero, the hero, receives his cosmic ascension, activating his third eye...deserved an imposing musical framework, befitting the importance of the events narrated. This volume thus became the most musically daring, the most experimental, and the one with the longest tracks. While each part was unique in its own way...and Angel's Egg had innovated with the short duration of its tracks and yet all its stylistic variety, You further developed these concepts, taking them a step further and becoming a classic not only for the band but for the genre itself.As the cover promises...there's a mix of spacey atmosphere and indigenous mysticism in Thoughts for Naught, Daevid Allen's composition, his ability to draw the rest into his universe...Tim Blake's synthesizers and Mike Howlett's bass in Magick Mother Invocation, creating that spacey psychedelia that always starts slowly...Didier Malherbe's saxophone, Gilli Smyth's vocals, and of course Pierre and Beno�t Moerlen's drums and percussion...plus Steve Hillage's ineffable and unmistakable guitar...everything will conspire to make that conjunction of stars explode in this volume.Master Builder is the construction of that curtain of synthesizers and the Buddhist choir...the percussion, the flute in an oriental orchestra...until the drums introduce the saxophone and the space rock jam...the cosmic French psychedelic free jazz begins...you can smell the 70s...you can feel it...there is precision, there is technique...yes...but there is also madness, freedom, anarchy, bohemianism, and that mix is ​​what made this Gong so special, ultimately, Allen's invocatory presence. When Hillage begins to play...nobody was prepared for that cascade of sound...for those doors that open in the mind with the notes of his sound...which, supported by the synthesizer, the drums and the bass, will make history.You is an album that wasn't rushed...in a decade that seized control of time to do with it as it saw fit for artistic purposes...and if this meant accelerating it to the point of confusion like King Crimson on Red...or slowing it down to the point of despair...like Gentle Giant on Free Hand...there was no doubt they were going to do it, and Gong took the time to build each step of ascent on You...because they knew that the feeling of climbing step by step is not the same as skipping steps in pursuit of a rush that only speaks of detachment from things.As layers of synthesizers build upon the drums in A Sprinkling of Clouds, and the drums with each hit seem to leap from the speakers and reach us as only a few records can...and the guitar sounds wild yet clean at the same time and you can follow its path at every moment...when Didier Malherbe joins in we understand why they distanced themselves from anyone who could do something similar and Frank Zappa's Inca's Roads didn't end up going in the same direction either.Perfect Mystery revisits the cabaret atmosphere of Angel's Egg only as a connection within the story, that oriental atmosphere that sets the stage for The Isle of Everywhere, one of the album's central themes...where synthesizers, Gilli Smyth's vocals, bass, and drums create an atmosphere reminiscent of King Crimson's Islands...only to then turn around and take another route, because Mike Howlett's swing on the bass had the necessary propulsion to soar without sopranos...and Gong sometimes has the ability to pass the third eye to us, if we can connect with his music; it's jazz...it's progressive rock...it's funk...it's psychedelia...it's the Canterbury scene, born in part because an Australian couldn't return to England and had to stay in France.Steve Hillage's solo begins so subtly behind the saxophone...but it does define itself throughout the entire development, supported by the bass and drums, at times playing with parts of jazz rock, until You Never Blow Your Trip Forever encompasses everything heard so far in the trilogy, even more psychedelic if possible...until it settles as if unintentionally into a section that, from improvised and played, culminates in another inspired song/prayer to the universe...a mantra repeated and destined to fade away, the complete opposite of this third volume of the most classic Gong which, as if it were a loop in time...must be repeated again and again once it has already ended.
items._cn_summary: GONG乐队1974年专辑《You》作为Radio Gnome Invisible三部曲的终章，融合了空间摇滚、迷幻音乐、自由爵士与东方管弦乐元素。专辑以合成器铺陈的氛围为基底，辅以萨克斯风的即兴演奏、佛教合唱团的人声层次，以及Steve Hillage标志性的吉他旋律。评论详细描述了《Master Builder》中东方管弦乐与空间摇滚即兴段的转换，以及《A Sprinkling of Clouds》里鼓点与合成器的层次叠加。这张专辑体现了坎特伯雷场景与法国迷幻音乐的独特交汇，具有较高的实验性与跨流派融合度，符合用户对实验前卫、自由爵士与世界音乐融合的偏好。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if a metronome were forcing its angle further and further outwards...expanding the range until it distorted...the trio, which didn't evoke the image of a trio, begins its second album with "A Visit to Newport Hospital," showcasing organ variations that sound like alarms, red alerts...Dave Stewart combines the magic of the 60s with the mysterious psychedelia that in the 70s would give way to that other Canterbury metric, and Mont Campbell with his measured vocals, plus the organ overlays from which the guiding threads would emerge, the solos of that melody which, as promised at the beginning, were nothing more than alarms of variation on the same note. Jazz and Bossa Nova are implicitly present...staining like raindrops on petals. The alarm awakens us.Contrasong features two tenor saxophones and two trumpets...the monotonous rhythm goes hand in hand with Mont Campbell's singing, and that piano that cuts through Clive Brooks' drums...which cuts through the trumpets...and cuts through the saxophones...and suddenly we're in uncharted territory...like that cover that looks like molten lead, whose solidifying shapes were once used to predict the future... where the trio that did not evoke the image of a trio preferred the mystery of the promise of what it suggests...but is not seen, what is, but is not yet known...an eternal advance, which postpones its realization with the concrete certainty of something that can be heard...can be felt...but not touched, and that when trying to understand it moves away, and comes closer if the mode of perception changes.Boilk is more variations, but in reverse...another way of confirming that intellectual understanding only sets us back...is by not understanding the proposed rules...which are reminiscent of Gy�rgy Ligeti and works like Atmospheres. When, in the final coda, Stewart's other great passion emerges with the Baroque religious organ.Long Piece No. 3 is the album's centerpiece, and here Bach's counterpoints become progressive, slicing through space until they become silence, and then a floating, sidereal space sustained by the drums. Here the trio plays at being a quartet, with the organ's bass lines, leading to an even more ethereal section with the piano...where, from atonal, they could become aggressive, provocative, but always maintaining the tension, that mystery of not knowing what will come next...what note, what chord awaits around the return of the nebula.The second part continues with the variations, the key to the album, creating spacey atmospheres...where that molten lead seems to solidify and take shape...but new suspended melodies, which distanced them from other bands of the genre, anchor them with that Hammond organ with one foot in the 60s, the same as Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother, but firm to the pattern that it is the organ that leads the race, this race without a visible final objective.The third part is considered the most complex, alternating between keyboard and piano, with the piano sections being the most virtuosic and classically accomplished. At times, it recalls the darker segments of Emerson, Lake & Palmer's Pictures at an Exhibition.The fourth and final part is even faster, related to Soft Machine's debut, but the jazzy Bossa rhythm with the keyboard cuts and repetitions, plus the bass and the out-of-tune keyboard, end up distancing it and solidifying this experiment of variations as the triumph of melodic harmony in all its forms.
items._cn_summary: 1971年Canterbury Scene先驱专辑，展现高度实验性和复杂性。融合自由爵士、先锋古典与Bossa Nova元素，编曲精密且留有即兴空间。器乐层叠丰富，organ与piano交织构建深邃氛围。Bach对位技术植入现代语汇，Ligeti式微音渐变与悬浮空间感贯穿全篇。"Long Piece No. 3"作为核心曲目，通过节奏切割与动态张力展现Jazz-Rock的先锋姿态。作品兼具学院派严谨与地下摇滚的粗粝质感，跨越半个世纪仍具前瞻性。

items.body: Dass von einigen Musikern gilt, dass sie stets mit neuen Ansätzen überraschen, mag selbst so eine Phrase sein. Bei Will Yates alias Memotone stimmt das in dem Punkt, dass er seinen Ansatz tatsächlich von Platte zu Platte verändert oder zumindest verschiebt. Ob das dann noch für Überraschungen taugt oder schon zur erwartbaren Konstante gerät? Was auf Warm Shadows ganz sicher unerwartet kommt, ist der Fortgang von Stück zu Stück. So lässt die Titelnummer am Anfang vermuten, dass Yates seine Klarinette erneut in verschiedenen Zusammenhängen erkundet, mit sich langsam vorantastendem Jazz und einer elektronischen Verfremdung des Blasinstruments, die an eine Verneigung in Richtung Jon Hassell denken lässt. Gleich im nächsten Song, ja, doch, singt dann die litauische Musikerin Ugnė Uma nach einem gesprochenen Monolog über verhaltenen einzelnen Gitarrentönen und einem ostinat im Hintergrund tackernden Rhythmus, der weniger Beat als durch diskretes Zittern tragende Zeitstruktur sein möchte. Der Beat versteckt sich auch in der folgenden Nummer, die man als Improvisieren mit Ambient-Elementen deuten kann, ohne dass klar ist, was für Instrumente da genau zum Einsatz kommen – Streicher? Echte? Konstant bleibt auf der Platte die friedliche Grundstimmung, die zugleich von unaufhörlicher Neugier getrieben scheint. Da kann man zwischendurch schon mal bei einer Indie-Rock-Nummer landen, die derart aufs Knappste arrangiert ist, dass sich beim besten Willen keine Rock-Klischees darin finden. Überraschung. Gute.
items._cn_summary: 英国音乐人Will Yates以Memotone为名创作的《Warm Shadows》展现了实验爵士与电子氛围的深度融合。专辑中单簧管被置于电子处理和即兴语境中，引用Jon Hassell式的第四世界音乐美学，同时与立陶宛歌手Ugnė Uma合作带来氛围化的演唱段落。作品在Ambient即兴、极简Indie-rock片段与电子声响之间游走，整体保持平和的基调和持续的好奇心驱动。评论指出曲序之间的变化出人意料，乐器配置模糊但呈现独特的声响设计。作为独立厂牌发行的小众作品，其跨界融合度和实验性高度契合偏好实验、前卫爵士、电子和世界音乐的听众。

items.body: We have Vancouver’s own Verboden Festival coming up this weekend in our backyard, and we’re excited about seeing a slew of familiar faves like SRSQ and Male Tears as well as catching acts we’ve been tracking through studio material but have yet to catch live, like Dildox and More Ephemerol. Hope to catch up with regular readers/listeners, too – should be a great weekend. On with this week’s tracks! Scimitar Street Sects, “No Percentage In Caution” The pair of LPs released by long-standing industrial punk terrorists Street Sects gave us a lot to chew on last year, and the band’s declaration that they’re moving in a “more rhythm based/song focused direction” with their new stuff is intriguing. This first sample clearly finds some of the harmonic and synth hook elements of the Full Color Eclipse second being drawn into a rhythmically tight package. No Percentage in Caution by Street Sects Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” We’ve come to associate Sydney Valette with a more continental and very French take on modern darkwave, avoiding many of the cliches of the style in favour of something that feels both classic, but without being beholden to the ur sources of the sound. New single “I Fucking Love You” holds with that, but sounds more strident than any of Valette’s work in recent memory. Partly it’s the tempo and push of the song, but also it’s a distinctly wounded and gothic vocal delivery, bringing out the emotion and drama here. If this is the direction of the new record, it could signal a nice shift into a new direction that would certainly be of interest to us as fans and followers of his work. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette Ortrotasce, “As I See It” Ortrotasce always keeps you on your toes; from single to single and within the run-time of the occasional longer release the one-man project deigns to release you’re never exactly sure where in the sprawling fields of synthpop, EBM, darkwave, and new beat things might land. You even have to keep your head on a pivot mid-track, as the peppy, Kraftwerkian programming of this early electro number is swiftly offset by a gloomy and resigned vocal which feels wholly separate. As I See It by Ortrotasce Transmigration, “Understanding” Last we checked in with the UK’s Transmigration, we noted their capacity to make the kind of gritty dark electro that benefits from obscurity and rough edges. New cut “Understanding”, the first taster from EP Living Information isn’t a huge leap away from that aesthetic, but it’s also a lot sharper and more direct, with atmosphere evolving out of the vocals, the speedy sequences and the aggression of the delivery, almost as a byproduct. The result is one of urgency, with a lot of the power stemming from how open and direct it all is, creating a sound that doesn’t need to be dressed up at all, arriving unforced, unadorned and hard-hitting. Living Information by Transmigration Scimitar, “Zenith (Inhalt remix)” Little bit of a ID:UD twofer this week with this Scimitar remix by Inhalt. We’ll be seeing the Los Angeles based band for the first time at Verboden this coming weekend, and we’re quite keen to do so; as an act we’ve tracked for a few years, they’ve consistently put out material that defies a lot of dark alt music trends, capturing sounds that are spiky, punky and uncompromising. And (spoilers) this week’s episode of We Have a Technical has Matia Simnovich of Inhalt as a guest, talking about the art of being a producer and what that entails. Tune into the latter, and then next week to hear our impressions of the performance from the former! Zenith (Inhalt Remix) by Scimitar Nikonn feat. MeLLLo, “Lighthouse” Lastly, something fairly off-format for us but still salient to our coverage. items.body: Are you ready to embark on a sonic adventure? Travelogue [Thailand] is the third in an ongoing series from the Touch imprint, in which two artists meet in a designated location and record an audio diary of their experience: first Nepal, then Bali and now Thailand. Over the course of nine days, CM von Hausswolff & Chandra Shukla visited multiple locations in Chaing Mai, from hotels to museums to temples, ending their journey in the Lanna Kingdom (Kingdom of a million rice fields) recording rivers, forests, monasteries and tribes. Sculpting all of these sonic treasures into four distinct pieces, the artists now present a portrait of Thailand in all its richness: miraculous, mysterious and multi-layered. “Nók Bpàa” eases the listener into the album with the overlapping sounds of the forest, traffic and a swiftly rising drone. A sudden rush – a motor? – interrupts the placidity. The artists admit that their diaries are not always calm, but contain “noise laden cacophony.” This uncertainty keeps the listener alert for the next sonic shift or juxtaposition: temple bells and monkeys, machinery and macaws. In this dense tapestry, alluring sounds emerge from the fog, only to be re-subsumed. In contrast, “Naga” leaps out of the speakers with rushing water and ceremonial song. One would have preferred a bit more rounding off at the start, but the piece soon becomes a study of dynamic contrast, falling into silence before introducing ripple, chirp and drone. The human element is far more apparent, children chattering, adults conversing, bells ringing, all folded into a backdrop of water and reverberation. Is this the real Thailand, or the sonic equivalent of “everything, everywhere, all at once?” The answer is somewhere in-between, as the album exudes a (pleasant) feeling of sensory overload. “Muaythai Changmai” begins with what sounds like a street festival, an expression of exuberance. Soon one encounters the sounds of the marketplace: loudspeaker announcements and a raucous crowd milling around. The introduction of English is startling, but momentary. A band begins to play, interrupted by another musician whose instrument sounds like bagpipes. Percussion cuts through the noise, then stops as the previous sound re-emerges. This is cacophony. Listening is like moving through the streets, drinking it all in. Balance is temporarily restored by the chants that begin “Wai Phra Kao Wat,” as spirituality is integral to any study of Thailand; for a few minutes, the album sounds like its cover. The temple gongs are no longer in the background, but in the fore. This piece deepens one’s appreciation of all that has come before, and its position as the closing track is wise. After all of the travels and the whirlwind of experiences, it is time to slow down and reflect. The forest sounds return, and the sense of peace is restored. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Within that tension between structure and collapse, Sven Piayda uncovers a strange sense of ease. Intercelestial thrives inside instability, shaping corroded electronics and broken rhythmic patterns into something fluid, tactile, and strangely alive. Rhythmic decay, fractured beat architecture Fragments of breakcore drift through Intercelestial, though never long enough to settle. Sven Piayda—also known as Record Of Tides—leans instead toward rhythmic decay, fractured beat architecture, and abstract funk currents stitched together through collage-minded sampling, murky 8-bit circuitry, and machine-driven pulse. Released only months ago, the record locks into a rare pocket of sound design, drawing strength from downtempo breakbeat patterns, melodic flickers, and warped digital haze, yet constantly pulling itself apart through groove-heavy disassembly and unstable rhythmic movement. It’s also important to highlight that this release—from Mahorka, based in Bulgaria—have once again produced a seamless and impressive work that is available in both digital and cassette formats. Tracks like “Superdusk,” “Filets,” “Dictionary,” and “Fish Tank” stand among the strongest moments here, each one balancing momentum with erosion. The opener “Nice Try” swarms with bursts of damaged frequencies and collapsing textures, while “Brother Love feat IG-75” channels an Aphex Twin-adjacent strain of melodic abstraction, unfolding like a forgotten trip-hop transmission caught in an endless loop—even the liner notes text elements come across as …I Care Because You Do inspired. Elsewhere, the trio of beach-themed pieces—“The Beach Crate,” “The Beach Shop,” and “The Beach Motel”—feels almost narrative in structure, sketching out a faded coastal memory through shuffled arrangements, detuned harmonics, and humid groove pressure. Their loose, drifting atmosphere illuminates Piayda’s instinct for combining fractured percussion with understated instrumental flow. Within that tension between structure and collapse, Piayda uncovers a strange sense of ease. Intercelestial thrives inside instability, shaping corroded electronics and broken rhythmic patterns into something fluid, tactile, and strangely alive. Even the cover artwork mirrors this sensibility: interlocking hexagonal forms folding into a surreal audiovisual mosaic that somehow clicks together with effortless precision. Intercelestial is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] Intercelestial by Record Of Tides

items.body: Awale Jant Band have released a live version of “Demon Na”, filmed at The Printworks, a Victorian live music venue on the America Ground quarter of Hastings. The studio single came out in November 2025 on AudioMaze, the second release of last year from London-based Senegalese vocalist Birame Seck and French guitarist and producer Thibaut Remy, ahead of their forthcoming album Gawlo Bi. Seck sings in Wolof and English, the lyric built around the experience of leaving and returning: “I’ve walked through France and England’s skies, touched Europe’s colours, heard many cries”. The title, “Demon Na”, is Wolof for “I have gone”, and the song makes that literal, tracing the narrator’s path from Senegal through Europe to America and back, carrying what that journey cost and what it taught. Ben Brown on drums and Karlos Seck on congas and djembe drive the rhythm, John Martin on tenor sax and George Jefford on trumpet above Mike Idowu‘s bass, with Remy’s electric guitar threading between the horns. Awale Jant Band take their name from the Wolof for “let the sun pass through”, a philosophy of cultural openness that extends directly into their personal histories. Frontman Birame Seck is the son of a gawlo, a griot in the Pulaar tradition, and the upcoming album, Gawlo Bi, takes its title from that exact heritage. The band have been building their London following for nearly a decade, appearing across the UK festival circuit, and 2026 sees them on the bill at Africa Oyé in Sefton Park, Liverpool on 20 & 21 June. items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the key players in the Ona Laietana (Laietan Wave) of Catalonian jazz fusion, ORQUESTRAMIRASOL was one of the earliest acts to emerge in the world of jazz fusion getting its start in 1973before the collapse of the Franco regime a couple years later. This group was amongst manyfusionists emerging from the Barcelona region with this band coming out of the nearby city of SantCugat del Vall�s with the band name resulting from a neighborhood in that city. The band releasedtwo well regarded albums in its short two year existence before morphing into a more Latin musicinfused offshoot called Mirasol-Colores. This debut SALSA CATALANA appeared on the Zeleste label andwas primarily inspired by the American fusion scene mining influences from the likes of Chic Coreaand Return To Forever as well as The Weather Report and Herbie Hancock. One of the more melodic and groovy of the Barcelona fusionists, ORQUESTRA MIRASOL eschewed the overtcomplex excesses of some of the most demanding European fusion acts and aimed to deliver moretraditional jazz structures intertwined into the context of progressive rock with both the lightairy aspects of The Weather Report in connection with the jazz funk styles of Herbie Hancock but asfar as the piano work goes the primary source of inspiration is clearly Chic Corea. In addition tothe foreign imports on board, this band eschewed the temptation of jumping n the Rock Andaluzbandwagon and instead looked towards the folk inspired sounds of the Mediterranean thus delivering asomewhat unique example of Spanish jazz fusion.The album is on the light and airier side of the equation. While not exactly commercial in nature inthe vein of Herbie Hancock's "Headhunter" with catchy funk grooves and ear wormy hooks, the band didblend its complexities in a fairly seamless manner which allowed an organic flow of ideas unlike thejitteriness of bands yet to come such as M�sica Urbana and others. The album features seven tracksand is quite short at only 33 minutes of playing time. The lineup included Xavier Batl�s (bass),Victor Ammann (piano), Ricard Roda (sax/flute/synthesizers), Pedrito Diaz (percussion), and MiquelLizandra (drums). The album makes full use of flute sounds offering some folk lightheadedness whilethe percussion delivers both the typical rock style of drumming as well as lots of Latin musicalcomponents and while not salsa as the album title might connote, the album does sound like the styleis intricately woven into the mix.Another aspect that this band was known for was that some of the keyboard parts were reminiscent ofEngland's Canterbury scene and at key moments refer to the works of 70s era Soft Machine but thebass grooves typically remain funk fueled but do venture off into a more hard bop stylistic approachas well. Notably absent are the sounds of guitars which exemplify the cleaner sound that the bandstrived for and although the bass and drums anchor it into the world of prog rock, the album's lackof heavy distortion makes it sound ethereal much like the band G�tic would deliver on its debutrelease down the road. It's an eclectic yet accessible style of fusion performed by this fascinatingband that despite its brevity delivered an exhilarating dose of high quality fusion that harkens toits references across the pond yet finding its own distinct methodology of blending it all together.One of the Spanish fusion acts that sounded more rooted in jazz than the rock elements. This is ahighly enjoyable debut.
items._cn_summary: 1974年加泰罗尼亚爵士融合专辑，展现Weather Report式的轻盈氛围与Herbie Hancock爵士放克风格的交织。乐队融合了前卫摇滚的结构性、Canterbury Scene的键盘编排以及地中海民谣元素，形成独特的西班牙爵士融合风格。专辑不含吉他，以干净的声场呈现 flute、sax 与合成器交织的层次感，融入了拉丁节奏元素。33分钟的7首曲目呈现流畅有机的发展脉络，兼具实验性与旋律性。来自西班牙非主流地区的独立厂牌发行，带有鲜明的地区文化特色。

items.body: Am Anfang war der Bass. Ayşe Hassan hat dem Power-Post-Punk der Savages um Jehnny Beth in den mittleren 2010ern mit ihrem Instrument jede Menge Dringlichkeit verpasst. Die ersten Sekunden von »Husbands« vergisst man ohnehin so leicht nicht mehr. Ihr erstes Soloalbum nimmt jetzt etwas den Druck raus. Als Esya nutzt sie kalte Maschinenmusik, Synthesizer und Drum Machines für einen Sound zwischen Industrial und Wave-Pop, versucht sich aber nicht an der unterkühlten Unnahbarkeit, die man hinter dem Mikro oft vermutet, sondern geht raus. Richtig raus. Das hat etwas Verletzliches, selbst dann, wenn Tracks wie »Heaven« pulsieren und sich beinahe überschlagen. Als Himmel bezeichnet sie hier die Clubs und Konzerthallen, deren Wände mehr Liebe und Hingabe gesehen haben als die meisten anderen. Auf Chasing Desire, für dessen sonnigen Keyboard-Beat Jessy Lanza verantwortlich zeichnet, wird sich Esya nicht ganz einig und singt insgesamt achtzehnmal »I (don’t) want to be your lover«. Was sie aber weiß und was dem Album sehr gut steht, ist der langsame Sog, der im Laufe der etwas über 30 Minuten entsteht. Die Drums verabschieden sich immer weiter in die zweite Reihe, was Highlights wie »Hiding Place« auf den Plan ruft, das im besten Sinne so klingt, als würde es die nächste Minimal-Wave-Compilation anführen.
items._cn_summary: Esya首张个人专辑延续其Savages时期的post-punk张力，但转向冷冽的机器音乐与合成器声响，风格介于Industrial与Wave-Pop之间。评论指出其放弃常见的冷淡疏离感，转而拥抱更具情感张力的表达。Jessy Lanza参与制作的阳光键盘节拍为专辑增添现代电子质感，而"Hiding Place"等曲目则展示Minimal-Wave的极简美学。整张专辑通过渐进式的声响构建，在30余分钟内形成缓慢而持续的吸引力。作为暗潮与电子音乐的跨界融合作品，其在传统暗潮框架内融入了当代电子制作的精致感，对于偏好实验电子与暗潮的用户而言具有较高契合度。

items.excerpt: Warp's IDM icons resurface after 13 years with a dark, disquieting record shaped by a violent world. Say goodbye to the fuzz and wistfulness.
items.body: Across their decades-long run as Boards of Canada, Marcus Eoin and Michael Sandison have drifted through endless shades of eerie. The Scottish brothers have been mischievous and playful, chopping up children's voices over downtempo hip-hop beats on their 1998 watershed Music Has the Right to Children and 2000's well-aged In A Beautiful Place Out In The Country. They've plunged into dark psychedelia with 2002's cryptic and sublime Geogaddi, tried melancholic pastoralism on for size in 2005 with The Campfire Headphase and teased out sinister undertones from queasy polyrhythms on 2013's lauded return to form Tomorrow's Harvest. With a penchant for backmasked samples and abraded synthesiser tones, the duo has historically thrived on obfuscation. This has in turn inspired a culture of eager exegesis among both fans and casual onlookers, heads tilted towards whatever they might pull off next. Their bleary, hypnotic records feel as much about what should be there as they are about what you can actually hear in the mix. Inferno shakes off its predecessors' shrouds, trading generalised unease for unadulterated menace. If Geogaddi continues to inspire robust discussion about its occultist allusions—it ends with a silent track to reach a runtime of precisely 66 minutes and 6 seconds—Inferno is more head-on, literally invoking demonic robot voices to read from Aleister Crowley's 1929 screed on human sacrifice. Its drumbeats and basslines slam against the ear, taking pages out of industrial and jungle's dog-eared playbooks. It's the darkest and most direct music ever issued under the Boards of Canada seal, a bold swing for an artist whose prettier early formula still inspires wan imitation to this day. The 18-track, 70-minute LP delivers its fair share of disguised utterances, but it also draws on plenty of clear speech with disarming transparency. A few of these samples stick to familiar discursive modes: "The Word Becomes Flesh" features a documentary narrator cheerfully describing the development of an embryo, a clip that could slot neatly onto Boards of Canada's turn-of-the-millennium offerings. Others highlight speakers who seethe with dramatic conviction. In "Age of Capricorn," in the midst of a smeary choral loop, an overpowering interjection comes from an American-accented voice deep in prayer: "I'm a sinner," he declares, his words hanging plainly in the ambience. "You bore my sin. You shed your blood for me, to cleanse me." Later, on "Father and Son," another believer speaks as if he's in the middle of a movie scene: "I love you, but I love the Lord more than any physical being," he repeats, his voice Auto-Tuned and snapped to the snaking beat. His conversation partner answers him in corroded metallic babbles reminiscent of Drukqs-era Aphex Twin. The Crowley excerpt on "All Reason Departs" opines in gravelly tones that "the great war must be fought. This bloody sacrifice is the critical point of the world-ceremony of the proclamation of Horus, the crowned and conquering child," before a dense, mechanic groove rolls through like the interlocking of several rusted gears. And on the pounding "Naraka," named after the realm of suffering in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions, we hear devotees chant the Hare Krishna mantra. It's easy to forget the song bears the name of a kind of hell. These are bleak expanses, to be sure. It's a heavy and at time unlovely listen, liable to jar on first contact. But there are oases to break up the wastes. "Into the Magic Land" draws upon Boards of Canada's early shoegaze influences with echoing guitar and cavernous percussion; "Deep Time," first released as April's "Tape 05," shimmers with plucked strings and wafting woodwinds. Close to the album's finish, "You Retreat in Time and Space" burbles with melodies so soft, so untroubled, that it could be drawn from lullabies. Bells twinkle. Horns blare. A beatific dawn settles over an empty plain, and terror retreats to dwindling memory. Against the turmoil of the current cultural moment, this is some of the most placid and enchanting music they've laid to tape. As Inferno’s crests from chaos to sanctuary, the rosy picture gives way to closer "I Saw Through Platonia," an understated coda to what are otherwise largely tense and writhing proceedings. The sound that predominates in the album's final minutes is the simple recording of a human heartbeat. With this sample, Boards of Canada pinch Inferno's themes to a subtle point. Throughout the record, people speak about what they believe to be true but cannot materially observe. They make declarations about deities. They talk about Christ's return as if it were sure to happen, a forewarning with an especially dire resonance in this age of Christofascist holy war. Here, after sharing glimpses of the world's unfolding horror intermingled with astonishing beauty, Boards of Canada drag your ear down to the sound of pulsing blood: a sound that anyone alive can hear within their own bodies. So many stories seduce, and so many are used to justify world-rending violence. What can we know to be real? The body exists. Start there.

tags: The Norwegian saxophonist is joined by Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim in a more rooted album of roots music
items.excerpt: A review of Camilla Hole Trio's Langs
items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track “Springleik,” signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close.
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: Camilla Hole Trio的新作《Langs》延续了上张专辑《Eventyrferd》的实验精神，将爵士乐、即兴演奏与挪威传统民间音乐进行跨界融合。乐团以女高音萨克斯为主线，辅以电子合成器和颤音琴的音色铺陈，构建出兼具学术气质与现代感的声景。三重奏的编排强调角色流动与即兴互动，避免了传统民间音乐直白的民俗展示，而是通过实验性的演奏方式重新诠释了挪威传统舞蹈音乐。电子元素的克制使用为作品增添了当代感，同时保持了与民间根源的连接。该专辑展现了北欧实验爵士乐在融合传统与现代方面的成熟探索，适合追求跨界创新的听众。

items.body:
I n the High Middle Ages, Hildegard of Bingen said that “The truly holy person welcomes all that is earthly.” William Blake declared in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790) that “Exuberance is beauty.” In 1855, Walt Whitman published the poem “Song Of Myself, 51” in Leaves of Grass , which contains the famous line “I am large, I contain multitudes.” I’m just skimming the surface of mystical experience, of those struck by wonder and an all-encompassing insight into how people fit into the ‘grand scheme of things.’ At some point on this trajectory, the boundary between the religious and the secular breaks down and simply being human becomes the ultimate wow. Which brings us to Polish artist Maria Ka’s latest album Di Mashin . Ka found that her family had Jewish roots, a discovery that led her to an immersion in Jewish studies and the Yiddish language. As on 2023’s Der Hemshekh , she unreels original songs written in Yiddish, embracing a politically active feminism and a committed meta-universality. Her musical vision is fragrantly mystical, and she presents us with a whole Yiddish cosmos. While not sharing the same type of musical style, Ka reminds me of John Zorn’s aesthetic of mixing the grotesque and the sacred into Jewish experimental music. She also reminds me of the woman on the phone sampled on Wally Brill’s Jewish cantorial electronica album The Covenant (2007), who confesses she can’t sleep after hearing someone in a bar talking about the Book of Ezekiel and being haunted by the vision of Jews arriving from a future space-time. She sees that we are all suspended in webs of relationships. She is also deeply aware of how we are subject to larger social forces and structures – which sometimes must be met with radical action -- that are the machinery of life. There is a heavy dose of electro and punkish attitude spinning through her musical universe. Ostensibly, the album is divided between electronic and rock tracks, but there is a consistency to the sound that is united in loopy joy. At its best, Di Mashin is sly and sexy. Opening track “Alef – Tsentauri Disko” finds Ka in the city, musing on the seaside, wriggling like a snake at night, and watching Gdańsk wake up. “I often Dream about Cosmos, about the Land above the Earth / overhead / Alef Centauri Jewish disco!” she sings, set to a thumping urban electro grind. (See video below)

“Vos iz dos?” is a standout, more in the ‘rock’ vein, with Ka howling a debate over the Yiddish language itself. Perhaps it is based in a critique that she received, as she starts with What is this? Maria, what is this? I constantly hear it, it has not finished You speak no Yiddish!/ It’s so easy! Your language is incorrect, mistaken is your speech and dialect! ” Given that Ka is producing new modern songs in Yiddish, there is something disarming in acknowledging the tension over who might claim ownership of language itself.

“SuperNove” might remind listeners of Jacob wrestling with God, if that battle was done to an ‘80s new wave beat. Ka has visions of the past, the Old World and old demons, and she fights a ghost that rises to block her way: “ I fought him with Strength, punched him with my both hands…I triumphed over him! I myself – I did triumph over him! ” And after that victory, “ it’s a great Surprise – the Past melted in the Cosmic Blast! ” Ka also seems to be challenging herself, pointing in new directions. “Di Kosmish motorn (Cosmic engines)” brought to mind the former Warsaw Village Band’s blues-influenced singer Maja Kleszcz. Depeche Mode’s (fronted by Dave Gahan, of Jewish ancestry) forays into fusing electronica with blues might be another touchpoint. Hearing the cosmic engines like a modern day Pythagoras, she is awestruck by hearing the cosmic engines in her head. “Dos geverk (The mechanism)” offers some grinding guitars to convey the constant motion of the daily rat race – echoed later on by the title track, “Di Mashin (The Machine),” which peels back the layers of society to reveal the incessant obsession for money. The music of ‘The Machine’ is hyperspeed cabaret, close to madness. The system demands more money – but she indicates that she is a spanner in the works, working to bring it down: “ I watch the machine’s death / Full and steadily red is my hand in the end. ”

Feminist politics come to the fore on “Ikh bin a froy (I am a woman),” and Ka reminds me a bit of the divine Ms. H of Bingen chanting over a motoric beat. She refuses to be hemmed in by structures, signaling that the Forest is her home, the stars her friends; “I wake up every day / and new scroll create.” Album closer “Di milkhome” (War)” is more future blues, transposing war, empty shipyards, and advice from her mother that all miseries will end and freedom will navigate the turmoil “like huge ships at Sea.” Di Mashin is possessed by such a singular offbeat vision and personal mythology that I wonder where Maria Ka will take her Yiddishfuturism next…Perhaps beyond our solar system, grooving on an interstellar plane with her band wriggling like snakes.
items._cn_summary: Maria Ka的《Di Mashin》是一张融合实验电子、朋克态度与世界音乐的中欧地下之作。专辑以意第绪语创作，涵盖都市电音节拍与摇滚张力，呈现出神秘主义与政治女性主义的交织。作品风格贴近约翰·佐恩式的sacred-grotesque美学，将犹太神秘传统与现代声响实验相融合，并带有暗潮与工业电子的侵略性底色。非主流独立发行，波兰艺术家背景为作品增添了东欧文化的独特视角。

items.body: B orn in Montreal, Haitian-Canadian musician-composer Jowee Omicil plays a fabulous variety of saxophones, clarinets, trumpets, flutes, piano, and keyboards. He came of age in the choral milieu of his father’s Montreal congregation, studied saxophone and music education at Berklee, and gleaned much from engagement with figures including Wyclef Jean, Tony Allen, Ibrahim Maalouf, Roy Hargrove, Kenny Garrett, Pharoah Sanders, Branford Marsalis, and Marcus Miller among others. Over the course of 2025, Omicil released sMiLes one song per month, each accompanied by a philosophizing podcast. The album opens with a striking reinterpretation of singer and Civil Rights activist Abbey Lincoln’s “Throw It Away,” whose message Omicil invokes in his voiceover, an expression of kinship in creative philosophical outlook. (For good measure, Omicil revisits the title on a distinctive “Throw it Away - FuLL oF LoVe Remix.”) Lincoln’s own 2007 rendition on Abbey Sings (Verve) offers critical context, itself worth a comparative audition for the original melody and the contemplative character of her lyrics. Throw it away, throw it away Give your love, live your life, each and every day And keep your hand wide open, let the sun shine through, Because you can never lose a thing, if it belongs to you. In less accomplished hands, the quirky sampling, effects, instrumentation, and wide-ranging, scruffy, sonic bricolage of sMiLes could make for one muddy mélange. But no danger lies here in Jowee’s paradoxical, provocative, sound-shifting extended groove. Omicil's voice and sax blend almost imperceptibly in “SOeuR FeLiX AKA BeeHive.” In “Trip to GHanA,” polyrhythm meets wah-tone high-life guitar, cackly sax, and wordless vocalise. Other titles transport the listener to Haiti, Morocco, Cape Verde, Jupiter, and Mali. “LeTTre Du MALi PouR JonaTHan” is a meditative, revelatory piano solo nearly ten minutes in length. sMiLes may invoke the free-blowing spirit of Miles (as on the sound-effected “MiLes ConvoY”), but there is no anxiety of influence here. Far from a rote genuflection to musical antecedents, the prevailing voice throughout is purely Omicil’s. As he counsels, “trust the note.” "Seek for the sound that is within you and the [instrument] will drive you to your destination… the singularity of sound is what I have always been searching for, the sound that comes from the heart, the sound that maybe, perhaps, is only heard in nature, this is what we are looking for when we are talking about sound… deep down, heartfelt uniqueness, always connected with the spirits…" - Jowee Omicil In accord with his music education formation, Omicil also leads music workshops through his BasH! AkademY, “a close-knit setting embracing spontaneity, authenticity, and shared growth,” which in 2025 included “a nomadic music experience traveling the world” to Mindelo, Cabo Verde. In 2026 Omicil will perform in New York, Canada, Martinique, France, Germany, Austria, Poland, Romania, the UK, and an African tour in the planning stage.
items._cn_summary: Jowee Omicil的专辑融合了学院派爵士、世界音乐与实验声响，体现了他与Pharoah Sanders、Kenny Garrett等大师的交流经历。专辑每首曲目配合哲学播客发布，采用古怪采样、效果器与声效应用构建scruffy的声音拼贴，从海地、摩洛哥到加纳、马里等地区的音乐语境中汲取灵感，并融入自由爵士的呼吸感与冥想式即兴段落。亮点包括对Abbey Lincoln名曲的重新诠释、近十分钟的沉思钢琴独奏以及融合非洲节拍与高保真吉他的实验性曲目。尽管部分段落可能显得过于折中，但对于追求跨界融合与声音实验的听众而言，这张专辑提供了丰富的听觉探索空间。

items.excerpt: A performance of David Dzubinski's 'Two Views of a Prayer'
items.body: I want to personally direct you to a remarkable piece of music titled "Two Views of a Prayer," composed and written by David Dzubinski as part of the Prism Quartet 's new series of collaborations called Unlocking Your Inner Composer . If you have listened to my radio programs, you are probably familiar with the quartet's ground-breaking, genre-blurring music. If not, there's no better introduction than this. Performed in November of 2025 at the Free Library of Philadelphia, they invited vocalist Ursula Rucker , percussionist Tyshawn Sorey , and violinist Carlos Santiago to collaborate on the arrangement and performance of Dzubinski's composition. It travels from raw to lyrical and back in the course of just under 4 minutes, with both finesse and energy. - Cliff Furnald, editor
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Prism四重奏与自由爵士名将Tyshawn Sorey、歌手Ursula Rucker、小提琴家Carlos Santiago合作，呈现了从粗粝到抒情的风格转变，融合了先锋四重奏、爵士即兴与现代作曲元素。Dzubinski的作品展现出跨界合作的实验性探索，四位音乐家的组合打破了古典室内乐与即兴爵士的界限。评论虽篇幅简短，但明确指出了作品的动态对比与艺术张力，适合偏好实验与学术爵士的听众。
